entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13091"/><div sID="gen24608" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13091"/><hi type="bold">2. they ... sent unto ... house of God--</hi>The Jews of the country sent to the house of God or congregation at Jerusalem. The altar was long since reared (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.3">Ezr 3:3</reference>), though the temple was not completed till two years afterwards (<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.15">Ezr 6:15</reference>). The priests' duty was to give decision on points of the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.9">De 17:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.2.4">Mt 2:4</reference>). Beth-el is here used instead of Beth-Jehovah, because the religious authorities, rather than the house itself (designated "Beth-Jehovah" in <reference osisRef="Zech.7.3">Zec 7:3</reference>), are intended. The old Beth-el had long ceased to be the seat of idol-worship, so that the name had lost its opprobrious meaning. "The house of the Lord" is used for the congregation of worshippers headed by their priests (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.7">Zec 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.1">Ho 8:1</reference>). Maurer makes the "house of God" nominative to "sent." Henderson makes "Beth-el" so.<div eID="gen24608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24609" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sherezer--</hi>an Assyrian name meaning, "Prefect of the treasury."<div eID="gen24609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24610" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Regemmelech--</hi>meaning, "The king's official." These names perhaps intimate the semi-heathen character of the inquirers, which may also be implied in the name "Beth-el" (Hebrew for "house of God"), so notorious once for its calf-worship. They sent to Jehovah's house as their forefathers sent to old Beth-el, not in the spirit of true obedience.<div eID="gen24610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24611" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pray before the Lord--</hi>literally, "to entreat the face of," that is, to offer sacrifices, the accompaniment of prayers, to conciliate His favor (<reference osisRef="1Sam.13.12">1Sa 13:12</reference>). <div eID="gen24611" type="x-p"/>

Should I weep in the fifth month--</hi>"I" represents here the people of God (compare <reference osisRef="Zech.8.21">Zec 8:21</reference>). This rather favors Maurer's view, taking "the house of God," the congregation, as nominative to "sent." Their hypocrisy appeared because they showed more concern about a ceremony of human institution (not improper in itself) than about moral obedience. If, too, they had trusted God's promise as to the restoration of Church and State, the fast would have now given place to joy, for which there was more cause than for grief [Pembellus].<div eID="gen24612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24613" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the prophets--</hi>Haggai and Zechariah especially. The tenth day of the fifth month was kept a fast, being the anniversary of the destruction of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.12-Jer.52.14">Jr 52:12-14</reference>). They ask, Should the fast be continued, now that the temple and city are being restored?<div eID="gen24613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24614" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">separating myself--</hi>sanctifying myself by separation, not only from food, but from all defilements (compare <reference osisRef="Joel.2.16">Joe 2:16</reference>) as was usual in a solemn fast. <div eID="gen24614" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13093"/><div sID="gen24615" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13093"/><hi type="bold">5. Speak unto all--</hi>The question had been asked in the name of the people in general by Sherezer and Regemmelech. The self-imposed fast they were tired of, not having observed it in the spirit of true religion.<div eID="gen24615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24616" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seventh month--</hi>This fast was in memory of the murder of Gedaliah and those with him at Mizpah, issuing in the dispersion of the Jews (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.25">2Ki 25:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.26">26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.41.1-Jer.41.3">Jr 41:1-3</reference>).<div eID="gen24616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24617" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">did ye ... fast unto me?--</hi>No; it was to gratify yourselves in hypocritical will-worship. If it had been "unto Me," ye would have "separated yourselves" not only from food, but from your sins (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.3-Isa.58.7">Is 58:3-7</reference>). They falsely made the fast an end intrinsically meritorious in itself, not a means towards God's glory in their sanctification. The true principle of piety, reference to God, was wanting: hence the emphatic repetition of "unto Me." Before settling questions as to the outward forms of piety (however proper, as in this case), the great question was as to piety itself; that being once settled, all their outward observances become sanctified, being "unto the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Rom.14.6">Ro 14:6</reference>). <div eID="gen24617" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13095"/><div sID="gen24619" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13095"/><hi type="bold">7. Should ye not hear the words--</hi>rather, "Should ye not do the words," as their question naturally was as to what they should do (<reference osisRef="Zech.7.3">Zec 7:3</reference>); "hearing" is not mentioned till <reference osisRef="Zech.7.12">Zec 7:12</reference>. The sense is, It is not fasts that Jehovah requires of you, but that ye should keep His precepts given to you at the time when Jerusalem was in its integrity. Had ye done so then, ye would have had no occasion to institute fasts to commemorate its destruction, for it would never have been destroyed (<reference osisRef="Zech.7.9-Zech.7.14">Zec 7:9-14</reference>) [Maurer]. Or, as the Margin, "Are not these the words" of the older prophets (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.3">Is 58:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.12">Jr 14:12</reference>) which threatened a curse for disobedience, which the event has so awfully confirmed. If ye follow them in sin, ye must follow them in suffering. English Version is good sense: Ye inquire anxiously about the fasts, whereas ye ought to be anxious about hearing the lesson taught by the former prophets and verified in the nation's punishment; penitence and obedience are required rather than fasts.<div eID="gen24619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24620" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the plain--</hi>southwest of Jerusalem. They then inhabited securely the region most unguarded. <div eID="gen24620" type="x-p"/>

entries.reader_content_plain: 14. whirlwind-- of wrath ( Na 1:3 ). nations whom they knew not-- foreign and barbarous. desolate after them-- after their expulsion and exile. It was ordered remarkably by God's providence, that no occupants took possession of it, but that during the Jews' absence it was reserved for them against their return after seventy years. they laid ... desolate-- The Jews did so by their sins. The blame of their destruction lay with themselves, rather than with the Babylonians ( 2Ch 36:21 ). pleasant land-- Canaan. Literally, "the land of desire" ( Jr 3:19 ).
